issues.title: --refarm-dir has no TypeScript counterpart, so the base guarantee is scoped to env-declared nodes
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS from the two-halves-one-node plan:

(c) `--refarm-dir` has no TypeScript counterpart: a node started with `--refarm-dir /srv/x/.refarm` and no env exports settles /srv/x, while the CLI answers $HOME, so the guarantee is scoped to env-declared nodes and is currently stated unconditionally.

DECIDED 2026-08-10 — SCOPE THE CLAIM, DO NOT MIRROR THE FLAG. Two ways to close this and only one of them is honest at this size:

Mirroring the flag means every CLI command grows a `--refarm-dir` and threads it through every resolver, because a base passed to one command and not another is worse than no flag at all. That is the centralisation slice (one resolved node scope, injected end to end), not a patch — and until it exists, a half-mirrored flag would make the two halves disagree in a NEW way while appearing to fix the old one.

What actually holds today, measured: `run_daemon` sets SOVEREIGN_BASE in-process from `--refarm-dir` before any config-node code runs, so the DAEMON and everything it spawns are consistent. A CLI invoked separately, in a shell without those exports, is a different process and cannot know what flag the daemon was started with. That is not a bug in the CLI; it is the boundary between two processes, and the honest form is to say so rather than to imply a guarantee that spans it.

So this item closes as a SCOPING correction: the guarantee is stated for env-declared nodes, and `refarm context` already reports which of SOVEREIGN_BASE / REFARM_HOME / home answered (cliBaseOrigin, now derived from declaredBaseWithOrigin rather than a mirrored ternary — ISS-025). An operator on a --refarm-dir node sees `home` there and can tell. The flag mirror is folded into the centralisation slice, where it costs one field instead of thirty.

issues.title: The budget re-query is unbounded on a hot path — UsageRecord is never reaped
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS QUEUE, opened at the operator's request on 2026-08-06:

(2) The budget re-query is unbounded and on a hot path: query-nodes filters by node TYPE not by
provider, and node_reap.rs's REAPABLE_TYPES omits UsageRecord so it is never pruned, so
system-wide volume drives it and once tripped the full fetch is a permanent per-call cost. Ways
out: host-side summing, or a provider-scoped query.

MEASURED 2026-08-11, on the operator's live node (~/.refarm/data/refarm/default.db, 276 KB):

     73  SessionEntry
     73  TaskEvent
     37  Task
     37  UserPrompt
     36  UsageRecord      <- this item's subject
     30  BudgetObservation
     10  Session

THE RE-QUERY DOES NOT FIRE TODAY, and cannot until this grows by three orders of magnitude. It
exists only for a TRUNCATED first read, and the first read asks for 10,000. Thirty-six rows do
not truncate. The "permanent per-call cost" the item describes is real in structure and has
never been paid.

That reframes the work rather than closing it. The growth is unbounded and the cost is a cliff,
not a slope: nothing degrades until the day the first read truncates, and from then on every
call pays a full fetch. But building for it now would be building for 36 rows.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE. Adding UsageRecord to REAPABLE_TYPES deletes SPEND HISTORY —
the exact rows the budget guard sums, and the rows `refarm budget observations` reports from.
node_reap.rs's own header states the rule that forbids it: a type "enters the allowlist only
alongside a live consumer, sized to that consumer's poll horizon". UsageRecord's live consumer
is the budget window (WINDOW_30D_NS in packages/agent/src/session/wasm_ops.rs), so a TTL here
would have to be comfortably beyond 30 days AND would still be destroying the operator's own
record of what he spent. That is a data-retention decision about his money, not a cleanup.

THE TWO REAL WAYS OUT, both needing a query-contract change (packages/plugin-wit):
  - PROVIDER-SCOPED QUERY. `query_nodes` filters by type only; a filter that also took a
    provider (and ideally a since-timestamp, since the window is 30 days) would make the read
    proportional to what the guard actually needs instead of to everything the node has ever
    recorded.
  - HOST-SIDE SUMMING. The host computes the windowed sum and returns a number. Smallest wire,
    largest behaviour change, and it moves arithmetic the agent currently owns and tests.

The since-timestamp is the more valuable half of the first option: the budget's question is
"spend in the last 30 days", and today it fetches all of history to answer it.

TRIGGER TO REVISIT, so this does not sit here as an opinion: when UsageRecord passes ~2,000 rows
on any real node, or when a first read is ever observed truncating. Re-run the count with the
query above.

VISIBLE HALF CLOSED 2026-08-11. `refarm budget observations|by-*|usage` now emit `completeness`
(complete|partial|unknown) beside `summary` on every --json surface, and the human notice derives
from the same shared judgement. The sums were already computed over a page that may have been cut;
what was missing was the sums SAYING SO to a consumer deciding "under budget".

The hot-path half is untouched and still gated on the same trigger recorded above: the re-query
cannot fire until UsageRecord volume grows ~3 orders of magnitude past the 36 rows measured on the
operator's live node.

issues.title: queryNodes returns a bare list, so eight consumers cannot tell a page from a table
issues.body:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-10, and the item's first claim is STALE while its second turns out to be the root of the whole family.

STALE: 'packages/sidecar-client reads only body.nodes and DISCARDS stored/truncated'. It does not. packages/sidecar-client/src/index.ts:141-148 reads both, refuses to default `truncated` to false or derive `stored` from nodes.length, and carries a doc comment stating the three-state rule. Fixed at some point after this item was filed on 2026-08-06.

STILL TRUE, AND LARGER THAN IT LOOKS: 'eight call sites still discard truncated'. They discard it because THE CONTRACT HAS NOWHERE TO PUT IT. packages/storage-contract-v1/src/types.ts:59 declares `queryNodes(type: string): Promise<unknown[]>` -- a bare list. Every consumer of that interface (tractor-ts, storage-node-view, barn's plugin ledger, farmhand, me-runtime, skill-capability, tractor-store) is STRUCTURALLY unable to know whether it received a page or the whole table. It is not eight independent oversights; it is one missing field, eight times.

MEASURED SHAPE: 17 call sites across 8 implementations of `queryNodes` -- farmhand, tractor-store, sidecar-client, storage-node-view, storage-rest, storage-sqlite, sync-loro, and the tractor-ts mock adapters. The sidecar-client is the ONE that already carries the fields, because it speaks HTTP and the HTTP body has them; the contract below it does not.

THIS ITEM IS THE ROOT OF GROUP F. ISS-044 (farmhand re-sorts Sessions by created_at_ns) cannot be closed before it: sorting the whole list and slicing is correct ONLY while the page is complete, and there is no way to check completeness through a contract that cannot express it. ISS-042 (no paging past MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE) and ISS-047 (the WIT returns a bare list<string>, the same silent ceiling one layer lower) are the same missing field at the HTTP and WASM boundaries.

SO IT IS A SLICE, NOT A FIX, and it needs its own spec and plan the way the ledger and probe slices did: change the contract to carry {rows, stored?, truncated?}, migrate 8 implementations, then let ISS-042/044/047 close against it with a fixture larger than each limit. Sizing it as a quick fix is how it would land half-done -- which is the state it is in now.

CONTRACT LANDED 2026-08-11 (spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-a-page-says-it-is-a-page-design.md,
steps 2-4). The root is closed; the migration deliberately is not.

WHAT SHIPPED, and the count that matters is that NOTHING was forced to guess:

  packages/storage-contract-v1
    QueryNodesPage { nodes, stored?, truncated? }   both facts optional, absent means absent
    readCompleteness(page) -> complete | partial | unknown       ONE judgement, was four
    StorageAdapter.queryNodesPage?(type, options?)               OPTIONAL, and that is the design
    auditPageCoherence / runQueryNodesPageConformance            the conformance the spec named

  packages/sidecar-client
    QueryGraphNodesResult now EXTENDS QueryNodesPage instead of restating it. The rule was written
    here first and lived here alone; two declarations that agree today can drift tomorrow, and
    extending turns that into a compile error. QueryGraphNodesOptions became an alias, because an
    interface that adds nothing is a second declaration pretending to be a first (the linter said
    so before the reviewer could).

  apps/refarm/src/commands/budget.ts
    the human notice branches on readCompleteness rather than on the raw field, and all three
    --json surfaces carry `completeness` beside the sums it qualifies.

WHY queryNodesPage IS OPTIONAL, since it will read as a hedge to whoever finds it next: fifteen
files implement StorageAdapter. A REQUIRED method makes every one of them invent truncated:false
-- the single value that must never be guessed. `queryNodesPage === undefined` is itself the third
state, in the type system: THIS ADAPTER CANNOT TELL YOU. Same idiom as Effort.workspace_source
riding beside workspace_id rather than replacing it.

STILL OPEN: no storage adapter implements queryNodesPage yet, and the 19 consumers still call the
bare queryNodes. They are not broken and no deadline forces them; each adopts when it has a reason.
The conformance is what makes adoption checkable rather than trusted -- an adapter that implements
the method and reports truncated:false while stored exceeds nodes.length FAILS it, which is the one
lie the type cannot prevent.

  sidecar/mod.rs:1760  tasks.sort_by(created_at_ns DESC)      a second sort order
  sidecar/mod.rs:1766  tasks.truncate(limit.min(100))         silent truncate
  sidecar/mod.rs:1768  { tasks, total: tasks.len() }          <- THE FOURTH

`total` to ask "is there more?" is answered "no", always. That is not a missing signal, it is a
wrong one — worse than the absent `stored`/`truncated` the item already names.

ALSO MEASURED: `get_task`'s fallback path does another unlimited `query_nodes("Task")` to do a
`contains` match on the id, and the status/session_id filters run AFTER the limit — the same
global-limit-then-filter shape ISS-045 just fixed in the agent, where it made an older task report
zero events.

Design, with the four changes and why removing `total` is safer than redefining it:
docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-a-page-says-it-is-a-page-design.md (step 5).

packages/tractor is a CLAUDE.md section 8 protected surface.

the fourth was never filed by anybody: `total` was computed AFTER the truncate, so it always
equalled the page size and answered "no" to every "is there more". REMOVED rather than redefined --

worse than leaving the endpoint alone: `?status=done` would answer out of the newest 100 rows of any

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-11 and CONFIRMED: NodesQuery carries `type` and `limit` and nothing else -- no
offset, no cursor. The contract half is now in place (ISS-040): QueryNodesPage has somewhere to put
the page facts, and readCompleteness is the shared verdict. What remains is the transport, and it
is spec step 6 -- `offset` on GET /nodes, in packages/tractor, a CLAUDE.md section 8 surface. Not a
cursor: cursors need a stable sort key no adapter guarantees today, and
docs/SOVEREIGN_RECORD_ORDERING.md is the document that would have to change first.

`NativeStorage::query_nodes_page` applies it in SQL. `MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE` STAYS -- the fix is
reachability, not removal of the ceiling.

`truncated` had to change meaning to make paging honest: it is `stored > offset + nodes.len()`, not
`stored > nodes.len()`. Rows before the offset were skipped on purpose and are reachable by asking
again; counting them as withheld would leave a caller paging forever, one empty page at a time. The
last page of a truncated read reports `truncated: false` even though `stored` still exceeds what it
carries. Pinned by its own test.

NOT A CURSOR, and the docs say so rather than implying otherwise: a cursor needs a sort key stable
under concurrent writes, which no adapter guarantees and docs/SOVEREIGN_RECORD_ORDERING.md would
have to settle first.

REACHED THE OPERATOR, which is the half that would otherwise have been invisible: `refarm budget
observations|by-*|usage` and `refarm tasks` all take `--offset`, and their truncation notices now
name the command and the number that reaches the rest. That notice had been WRONG TWICE in opposite
directions -- first "raise --limit" (which could not work), then "not reachable today" (true when
written, false the moment offset shipped) -- so it now names a runnable command, which is the only
form of the claim that goes stale loudly.

item in this repository to be arguing against code that had already changed.

  packages/windmill/src/local-scheduler.js   a cron evaluator, and it is not a sketch:
      - the five-field form, plus @hourly/@daily/@weekly
      - THREE STATES already: due / declared / unsupported (D4, satisfied)
      - the day-of-month vs day-of-week OR rule CORRECT (the trap ISS-076 was filed about)
  packages/windmill/src/local-scheduler-ledger.js   fire-once, so repeated ticks are idempotent
  packages/cli/src/scheduled-work-runner.ts         the composition seam D1 asks for
  refarm project automations tick [--submit]        a host that ticks, on demand

the contract, echoed back in every job description, and READ BY NOTHING. A nightly job in
America/Sao_Paulo answered `declared` at midnight in Sao Paulo and `due` at nine in the evening,
while reporting the zone as if it had been honoured. Fixed the same day -- see the commit.

this node -- no systemd timer (only refarm-web-serve.service), no crontab, nothing in the repo, and
no periodic loop in the daemon. The executor is complete and unreached.

TWO WAYS TO CLOSE IT, and the choice is the operator's:
  (a) the daemon's own loop, which is spec D1 and packages/tractor (a section 8 surface). It is the
      right long-term home -- the daemon already holds the effort store, resolves budgets and
      writes observations, so an automation run costs nothing extra to govern.
  (b) a systemd user timer calling `refarm project automations tick --submit`. The node already
      runs exactly this arrangement for refarm-web-serve, it is reversible in one command, and it
      proves the whole path end to end before any Rust is written.

(b) is not a worse (a). It is how you find out whether the loop is the hard part before building
the hard part, and D5's missed-window reporting is easier to get right with a supervisor that
records its own misses.

issues.title: Which cron parser? None exists, the repo is dependency-light, and cron is subtly easy to get wrong
issues.body:
Which cron parser? None exists, this repo is deliberately dependency-light, and cron is subtly easy to get wrong (day-of-week versus day-of-month). Vendoring something tested likely beats hand-rolling, and the choice deserves the same source-and-date discipline every other external dependency here now carries.

ANSWERED BY RE-MEASUREMENT 2026-08-11, not by a decision. "None exists" was false: the parser is in
packages/windmill/src/local-scheduler.js, hand-rolled and zero-dependency.

AND IT ALREADY GETS THE TRAP THIS ITEM WAS FILED ABOUT. Day-of-month versus day-of-week: when BOTH
fields are restricted, cron matches EITHER, not both. The implementation reads
`domDue || dowDue`, with the two single-restriction cases separated above it. Correct, and now
pinned by a test that says so in words rather than leaving the next reader to re-derive it.

SO NO DEPENDENCY IS NEEDED, and the reason is stronger than "we already wrote one". Every cron
library answers "when is the next occurrence" or throws. This repository needs THREE STATES --
due / not due / undecidable (spec D4) -- and a thrown exception swallowed by a catch is precisely
how "undecidable" becomes "not due", which is the daily-handoff failure that opened ISS-066. A
vendored parser would still need our own three-state layer on top of it, so the dependency would
buy parsing we already have and none of the part that matters.

WHAT THE PARSER DOES NOT DO, recorded so nobody assumes otherwise: no `@yearly`/`@monthly`/
`@reboot`, no step-on-range (`1-9/2`), no month or weekday NAMES (JAN, MON), no `L`/`W`/`#`. Each
of those returns `unsupported` rather than a wrong answer, which is the safe direction. Add one
when an automation needs it.

issues.title: rcdc5 automation is blocked on P1: a pending prompt's lifetime is its asker's, and nothing resumes an effort
issues.body:
rcdc5 as a workspace-scoped automation consumer is BLOCKED on two named pieces, and the blocker is a declared principle rather than an oversight: pending_prompt.rs states P1, `a pending prompt's lifetime is its asker's lifetime, nothing persists`, and nothing resumes a persisted non-terminal effort. Until both change, an automation that waits for an MFA push cannot survive a restart, and 'waiting for a human' is indistinguishable from 'dead'.

HALF CLOSED 2026-08-11, and the half that closed is the sentence this item is named for:
"waiting for a human" is now distinguishable from "dead".

WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, and it reframed the work: the trail has ALWAYS remembered decisions
durably -- `OperationRecord` in a JSON file, matched by `standingDecision`, which is what stops a
wizard re-asking something already settled. What nothing remembered was a question STILL WAITING.
So a background run that asked and died left no trace of having asked, and its next run asked
again. That is the operator's own complaint about the VPN, one layer above the prompt hub.

    decision made      -> durable
    question waiting   -> died with the asker

SHIPPED, in @refarm.dev/operation-consent-v1:

  OperationQuestion             asked, not yet decided -- requestId, purpose, requester, expiresAt
  standingQuestion()            PURE: outstanding | expired | none
  OperationTrail.readQuestions? OPTIONAL, so a trail that cannot remember says so by absence
  runOperationConsent           records BEFORE asking, closes in a `finally`, and returns a new
                                `already-asked` outcome instead of publishing a second card

P1 IS NOT WEAKENED and was not touched. `pending_prompt.rs` keeps its principle exactly -- a
PROMPT's lifetime is its asker's, nothing persists, no garbage collection, no stale-answer
problem. This is a different record in a different place: the prompt still dies with its asker;
the memory that it was asked does not. That is the "second kind of prompt" the automation spec's
D9 named as the alternative to revisiting P1, and it turned out to belong in the consent trail
rather than in the hub.

EXPIRY IS BY TIME, NEVER BY SWEEPING. A run killed outright cannot close its own record, so the
record carries the asker's deadline (24h default) and reads as `expired` past it -- which falls
through and asks again ON PURPOSE. A record that blocked the question forever would turn one
`kill -9` into permanent silence about that operation.

STILL OPEN, and it is the other half this item names:

1. THE ANSWER IS STILL EPHEMERAL. `runOperationConsent` writes the decision record in the ASKING
   process, so an operator answering after that process is gone has nobody to write it down. The
   durable question means the next run knows not to ask twice; it does not yet mean the answer
   survives. Closing that needs the node to record the decision itself -- Rust, and a real design
   decision about who owns the write.

2. NOTHING RESUMES A PERSISTED NON-TERMINAL EFFORT. Untouched. `load_persisted_efforts` restores
   the state at boot and nothing picks it up.

THE OTHER HALF CLOSED 2026-08-12. A question whose asker is gone can now be answered, and the
answer TAKES EFFECT.

WHAT THE FIRST DESIGN GOT WRONG, found by asking what a recorded decision actually does: a
decision and its application happen TOGETHER in operation-consent-v1, and `already-decided`
deliberately does not re-apply. So recording an answer out of band would have produced a decision
that never took effect -- worse than being unable to decide, because it looks like it worked.

The fix is that the standing question carries the WHOLE REQUEST, not just what a surface needs to
display it. A request holds its own `changes`, with a complete before/after per file, which is
exactly what applying it later needs.

    refarm resume --answer <id> --authorize|--decline

--authorize and --decline are both required to be explicit. A missing flag is not "probably yes"
and not "probably no"; it is a malformed instruction, and the answer is the one thing a consent
surface must never guess.

AND IT IMPLEMENTS ISS-118's SECOND CHECK. Before applying, every change's `before` is compared
against the file as it is NOW. Any drift refuses with `stale` and names the files: the gap between
asking and answering is exactly where a card sits on a phone for an hour, and the operator
authorised a change to the file they were SHOWN, not to this one. A refused answer leaves the
question standing, because nothing was decided.

Five states, and only two of them are ordinary: applied, declined, expired, unanswerable (a record
written before requests were stored -- reported honestly rather than offered a button that fails),
and stale.

STILL OPEN, and it is now a smaller thing than this item started as: nothing resumes a persisted
non-terminal effort. `load_persisted_efforts` restores the state at boot and nothing picks it up.
That is a different mechanism from consent and does not block the VPN case any more.

     `refarm check --next-action --json` -> ok: true, recommendations: [].
  4. Same clean tree, `refarm health --json` -> config_node_drift IS present:
     "graph node revision sha256:334404f2... differs from local sha256:6d..." (twice), alongside
     stale_build findings.

So the divergence exists on this node REGARDLESS of the working tree. What changes with the working
tree is whether the mandated entry point LOOKS: `refarm check --next-action --json` runs the
"affected" profile (selection.profile: "affected", validationScope: "dirtyTree"), and a change under
.project/** pulls the config-node auditor in while a change under docs/ or README.md does not. The
result is that a real, standing node defect reports ok: true from the command CLAUDE.md tells every
agent to trust, and only becomes visible if the slice happens to touch the right path.

Two states where three are needed, one more time: "audited and clean" and "not audited" produce the
identical ok: true. The third state -- "this auditor did not run for this change set" -- is not
reported anywhere in the envelope. Note the auditor itself already got this right one layer down: it
distinguishes config_node_unreachable ("could not check") from a clean pass, precisely so a failed
read cannot read as fine (packages/health/src/auditors/config-node.js:150-168). The selection layer
above it then re-introduces the collapse it was written to avoid.

THE NODE CONDITION UNDERNEATH, recorded so it is not lost with this item: the graph's RefarmConfig
node and ~/.refarm/config.json disagree, which is the expected consequence of the 2026-08-08 node
update (ISS-067 -- connections.ovpn-serpro, trusted_plugins and approvedPermissions were written to
the operator's real config) with nothing re-syncing the graph node afterwards. The remedy the
recommendation names is "Re-run the runtime to re-sync the RefarmConfig node" -- a restart, which is
the operator's call because it interrupts whatever the node is serving, exactly as the handoff
already says of the other restart-shaped findings. It was deliberately NOT done by the slice that
found it.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE (not taken here): either the check envelope reports which auditors were skipped
for this change set, or the config-node audit is unconditional because node-state findings are not a
function of which files a slice edited. The second is the smaller change and the honest one -- a
node's config drifting has nothing to do with the diff.

CORRECTED 2026-08-09 (fix round 1) — THE PRECEDENCE CLAIM ABOVE WAS WRONG, AND THE EXPERIMENT COULD
NOT HAVE PROVEN IT. The paragraphs above read the stash experiment as showing the drift "exists on
this node REGARDLESS of the working tree" and therefore predates this slice. `git stash` moves files
inside the REPOSITORY; ~/.refarm/config.json is outside it and was never touched by any of those
four commands, so the experiment could not distinguish "pre-existing" from "caused by an edit made
outside the repository". It was the second: the controller edited ~/.refarm/config.json before Task 4
to declare this workspace's ledger, and nothing re-synced the RefarmConfig graph node afterwards.
Step 4 (health on a clean tree) shows only that the drift is not a function of the working tree —
which is true, and is a weaker statement than the one it was used for.

WHAT SURVIVES THE CORRECTION, unchanged and still the reason this item is open: steps 1-4 measured a
real REPORTING asymmetry. `refarm check --next-action --json` returned ok: true on the same node, at
the same moment, at which `refarm health --json` reported config_node_drift — because check's
affected profile pulls the config-node auditor in only when the change set touches .project/**. The
cause of the drift is irrelevant to that; a node-state finding is not a function of which files a
slice edited, and "audited and clean" still cannot be told from "not audited" in the envelope.

RESOLVED PART: the operator restarted the runtime on 2026-08-09. The graph node re-synced, the drift
is gone, `refarm check --next-action --json` returns ok: true, and both agent lanes pass. The restart
itself surfaced ISS-084 — `refarm runtime restart --json` reported ok: false with a null error for a
restart that had succeeded.

issues.title: runtime restart --json reports ok:false with a null error after a restart that succeeded
issues.body:
REPORTED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-08-09, while clearing the config drift that ISS-083 describes.
`refarm runtime restart --json` returned, verbatim:

  {"ok": false, "error": null, "message": null, "nextAction": "refarm runtime ensure --wait --next-command"}

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: the restart SUCCEEDED. Following the handoff confirmed the runtime ready and
the RefarmConfig drift gone; `refarm check --next-action --json` returned ok: true afterwards. So the
command reported failure for an act it had just performed, with a null error and a null message —
unreadable to an operator and unreadable to an agent, which under CLAUDE.md's JSON handoff rules is
told to inspect `ok` and follow `nextCommands` before deciding anything.

THE MECHANISM, read from the code rather than guessed:

  - apps/refarm/src/commands/runtime.ts:235-238 — after spawning, `ready` is probed ONLY when
    --wait is passed: `const ready = opts.wait ? await waitForRuntimeReady() : undefined`.
  - :244-248 — the JSON payload is then built from `{...payload}` with `ready` spread in only when
    it is not undefined. Without --wait, `payload` is the snapshot taken by
    `resolveRuntimeStartCommand` BEFORE the restart — i.e. describing a runtime that had just been
    stopped one statement earlier.
  - apps/refarm/src/commands/runtime-status.ts:181-190 — `runtimeOperationOk` judges a restart with
    `runtimeIsHealthy(payload)` (`activeEngine !== "unknown" && !issue && ready !== false`). Against
    a pre-restart snapshot that verdict is about a state that no longer exists by the time it prints.
  - :263 — `if (opts.wait && !ready) process.exitCode = 1`. So without --wait the envelope says
    `ok: false` while the process exits 0: the two channels disagree about the same run.

WHY `error` AND `message` ARE NULL: this envelope carries the runtime's state under `issue`, not
under `error`/`message`, so those keys are emitted as null for every restart. A consumer reading
`ok: false` finds nothing that says WHAT failed, because nothing did.

THE SHAPE: two states where three are needed, again. "The restart failed" and "nobody looked after
the restart" produce the identical `ok: false`. `status` already got this right one function up —
runtime-status.ts:167-179 documents at length why a report is always `ok: true` and why acts are
judged by health — but an act whose result was never observed is a third state that reasoning does
not cover: not healthy, not unhealthy, UNOBSERVED.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE (not taken here): either re-probe readiness before judging a restart even
without --wait, or report `ok` for the ACT (the stop and the spawn both succeeded) and leave
readiness to `ready`/`issue` where a caller can see it — with `ready: null` meaning unobserved
rather than false. The second matches this repo's own precedent that an unobserved value is not a
negative one. Whichever is chosen, `ok: false` with a null error and a null message must not survive.

Correcting an existing item's prose is still a hand edit of a governed document, the exact writer-gap shape that killed the ledger the first time (docs/WORK_ITEM_LEDGER.md section 7: tasks.json, issues.json and requirements.json had no writer, so nobody edited them, so every check on them stayed green over a record nobody was updating). axis used to be on this list too; set-axis was built during this branch specifically because reclassifying two legacy items required writing the document by hand otherwise. title/body/location remain unclosed. issues.title: The postcss security pin is overtaken by a newer advisory, the same drift that hit js-yaml
issues.body:
RESOLVED 2026-08-11. The pin was stale exactly as this item described, and the fix is the second
of the two it named: rewrite it in the boundary style so the next drift is legible.

  was:  postcss@<=8.5.17: ^8.5.18     boundary from an older advisory
  now:  postcss@<=8.5.22: ^8.5.23     the boundary GHSA-fxqj-rqcc-2cmp actually states

  lockfile: 8.5.22 (INSIDE the vulnerable range, with a pin sitting above it) -> 8.5.26

Verified against the npm registry, not only the advisory page: 8.5.23 is published and 8.5.26 is
latest on the 8.5 line. `^8.5.23` keeps the same major, matching the nanoid entry's reasoning.

WHY BOUNDARY STYLE AND NOT JUST A BUMP, which is what this item asked to decide: a `<=X: ^Y` pin
whose X is not the CURRENT advisory boundary reads as protection and is not. Bumping X alone
fixes today; stating the boundary the advisory states makes the NEXT drift readable without

Verified after: `turbo run build` 139/139, `turbo run test` 282/282.
`pnpm audit --audit-level=moderate --prod` drops postcss from its list.

issues.title: The decompress advisory is accepted on the grounds that it has no patch, and a patch now exists
issues.body:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-11, and THIS ITEM WAS WRONG — in the same way as the comment it was
correcting, and for the same reason.

The item says: "pnpm audit reports decompress <=4.2.1 -> patched >=4.2.2 ... The no-patch half of
the recorded justification is now FALSE."

  npm view decompress versions   ->  41 versions, ending at 4.2.1
  npm view decompress dist-tags  ->  latest: 4.2.1
  override to ^4.2.2             ->  ERR_PNPM_NO_MATCHING_VERSION

THERE IS NO 4.2.2. The `patched >=4.2.2` in `pnpm audit` is ADVISORY METADATA — a statement about
which version WOULD carry the fix — not a claim that it exists. The original justification's
central sentence was true, and this item disputed it by reading the same metadata the comment's
author had read. Neither asked the registry. That is the lesson worth keeping, and it is now
written into the exception itself.

WHAT WAS TRUE, and is corrected on the record:

  1. THE SEVERITY IS CRITICAL, not moderate. That is why `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` exits 0
     while its own metadata reports `critical: 1` — the count includes what ignoreGhsas
     suppresses, the gate does not.

  2. THE SUPPRESSION DOES NOT SUPPRESS. GHSA-h39j-r5qq-r9mm reports the SAME package, range and
     (absent) patch, and is not on the list, so decompress fails the moderate-prod gate anyway.
     The ignore hid the severity and bought nothing. It is deliberately NOT extended to the
     sibling: silencing a real finding with no available fix is a different act from accepting
     one.

  3. THE DEV-ONLY REACH IS NOW VERIFIED, which this item correctly noted had never been
     re-checked. `pnpm why decompress -r` resolves exactly one path:
     decompress@4.2.1 <- @bytecodealliance/weval <- componentize-js <- @bytecodealliance/jco —
     the build-time WASM toolchain. It does not reach a shipped artifact.

THE EXCEPTION STANDS, with its justification rewritten to say all of the above and to name the
trigger: a published decompress >4.2.1, or jco dropping weval. Re-check the REGISTRY, not the
advisory page.

issues.title: CI audits at three different scopes and the moderate-prod one is red
issues.body:
RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by the operator's ruling: **`pnpm audit --audit-level=moderate --prod` is the
gate, with a re-check date on every accepted advisory.** Option (c) of the three this item listed.

WHAT WAS TRUE AND IS NOW ANSWERED: four audit invocations ran at three scopes and nothing said
which one had to hold. `--audit-level=high` passed while `moderate --prod` failed, so "the audit
is green" named no particular fact. `before-push`'s security step was the `high` one; it is the
moderate gate now.

WHY THE DATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, and not a refinement: four advisories fail this scope and none
has a reachable fix, so a bare `moderate --prod` is red on arrival — and a gate red on arrival is
one an operator learns to bypass. The two mechanisms that solved that before both accepted things
FOREVER, and both went stale with their justifications still sitting there looking current:
the postcss pin (ISS-086) and a CRITICAL `ignoreGhsas` entry whose own comment admitted it had
not been re-verified (ISS-087).

SHIPPED:
  scripts/security/accepted-advisories.mjs  the five acceptances, each with WHY, a TRIGGER, and
                                            a recheckBy date
  scripts/security/audit-gate.mjs           the gate
  pnpm run security:gate                    also wired into `refarm agent finish --lane before-push`

FOUR WAYS TO FAIL, and only the first is what a security gate normally has. All four proven by
poisoning a live run:
  UNACCEPTED  reported and undeclared                     (removed an entry -> named it)
  EXPIRED     accepted, still reported, date passed       (moved a date back -> exit 1, and the
                                                           message prints that entry's TRIGGER,
                                                           so it says what to re-check)
  STALE       accepted and no longer reported             (the exception outlived its advisory)
  HIDDEN      severity counts do not reconcile

HIDDEN is this item's sharpest observation made mechanical. `pnpm audit` COUNTS an ignoreGhsas
advisory in `metadata.vulnerabilities` and OMITS it from `advisories`, which is why
`--audit-level=high` exits 0 while printing `critical: 1` in the same JSON. The gate adds the
declared `suppressed` entries back and fails on any surplus — so the suppression is no longer
invisible, and a silenced advisory nobody wrote down is as loud as a brand-new one.

CURRENT STATE: 4 reported, 5 declared (4 reported + 1 suppressed critical), next re-check
2026-10-10. Gate green.

  turbo run build 139/139 · turbo run test 282/282 · before-push green end to end

issues.title: The operator requirements R1-R12 exist only in Markdown and are invisible to every instrument

Eleven are Parcial and one (R12, the executive view) is Ausente. NONE of them exists in .project/requirements.json. issues.title: A work item cannot declare which operator requirement it serves
issues.body: issues.schema.json sets additionalProperties: false and models no requirement field, so an item cannot say which operator requirement it serves. The reverse direction does not work either: scripts/ci/project-block-consistency.mjs:192 validates requirements.traces_to against task ids and phase numbers ONLY, so a requirement cannot point at a work item.
