issues.title: refarm task list --json writes to the node on every read
issues.body: MEASURED 2026-08-10 while closing the footguns before the directory-independence burn-down. A sweep of 72 read-only invocations (the 36 probeable commands, run twice each from the repository) changed exactly one file on the operator's real node: ~/.refarm/sessions/task-session.v1.json. Bisected to a single command: `refarm task list --json` rewrites it on every read, updating `updatedAt` and stamping `lastCommand: "list"` (size unchanged 9648 -> 9648; only mtime and those fields move). WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: (1) it makes a read command a writer, so the node's task-session record cannot distinguish 'this effort was touched' from 'somebody listed'; `lastCommand` and `updatedAt` are written by an observer, which is the same shape as a report that claims more than it measured. (2) It is a live hazard for scripts/directory-independence.mjs, which runs every probed command once per directory plus a control run -- a mutating entry would write to the operator's real node three times per probe invocation, forever, and the probe is meant to be run often. THE READ-ONLY RULE HAD NO OBSERVATION BEHIND IT: `task list` is called list, it prints, it exits 0, and it looks read-only from every angle a reviewer has. That is why the probe now snapshots the sovereign dir around a full run and WARNS naming the files that changed (warn, not block: the daemon shares that directory and may write concurrently, and a check that fires on the environment trains its reader to ignore it). UNTIL THIS IS FIXED, `task list` is excluded from PROBE_COMMANDS with this id as the reason -- so 1 of the 36 probeable invocations is deliberately unmeasured, named rather than silently dropped. FIX SHAPE: the read path should not persist; if a read genuinely needs to refresh a cache, that write belongs behind an explicit flag or a separate verb, not inside `list`.

issues.title: refarm resume --json returns ok:true with an EMPTY project block outside the repository
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Sixteen diverging field paths: project.blockers, project.context, project.currentPhase, project.currentTasks, project.nextActions, project.openQuestions, project.path, project.timestamp, and all eight project.truncation.{blockers,currentTasks,nextActions,openQuestions}.{returned,total}. Directories: /home/s095407044/github/refarm vs /tmp vs ~/git/rcdc5. environmentPressure.signals was EXCLUDED as time-variant by the control pair, so all sixteen are real.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY RETURNS from /tmp, measured: ok:true, project.path null, currentPhase null, context empty string, 0 currentTasks, 0 nextActions, 0 blockers, truncation null.

THIS IS THE ZERO THAT IS NOT A ZERO, at the front door. CLAUDE.md section 4 mandates 'refarm resume --json' at the start of EVERY slice and tells the agent to trust its nextCommands. From outside the repository it reports no work, no blockers and no next actions with ok:true, and nothing in the envelope distinguishes 'this node has no pending work' from 'I did not read any project'. Worse: the truncation field is null -- the field the 2026-08-08 slice added SPECIFICALLY so a partial read could not masquerade as a complete one now reads as 'nothing was truncated' rather than 'nothing was read'. That slice fixed the instrument lying about 5-of-24; this is the same instrument lying about 0-of-24 one directory over.

SCOPE DECISION, AND WHY IT IS A CONVICTION RATHER THAN A DECLARATION: resume is MIXED. Runtime, model, session and ledger are node facts -- the ledger block is correctly identical from all three directories, which proves the node path works -- while the project block is genuinely this directory's project. Declaring project.* as allowed-varying would make the row pass and leave the empty-block-with-ok-true untouched, which is declaring the defect instead of closing it.

FIX SHAPE, to be decided in the burn-down after auditing the call sites: the project block needs three states, not two -- a project was read (contents), there is no project here (explicitly absent, never an empty list), and the project could not be read (a named failure). apps/refarm/src/commands/resume.ts carries 3 bare process.cwd() sites, and packages/cli/src/project-handoff.ts:100 resolves .project/handoff.json as a RELATIVE path -- the same positional resolution the ledger slice named when it refused to mirror 'refarm project' for the issues command.

issues.title: doctor reports host.packageManager as pnpm here and npm from anywhere else
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field paths: host.packageManager, nextAction, nextActions, nextCommand, nextCommands, recommendations, warnings, warningCount.

MEASURED VALUES: host.packageManager is 'pnpm' from /home/s095407044/github/refarm and 'npm' from BOTH /tmp and ~/git/rcdc5.

THE FIELD NAME IS THE ARGUMENT: a field called host.* cannot depend on which directory the operator is standing in. Either the value is the project's package manager and the name is a lie, or the resolution is wrong. Both are defects and they are not the same defect.

The seven other diverging fields are DOWNSTREAM: nextAction, nextCommands, recommendations, warnings and warningCount are derived from the wrong packageManager, so the doctor's ADVICE changes with the caller's directory too. That is the part that costs -- 'refarm doctor' is what an operator or agent runs to be told what to do next, and it currently says something different depending on where you were standing when you asked.

THE RATCHET'S LARGEST CLUSTER IS BEHIND THIS: packages/config/src/package-manager.js carries TEN bare process.cwd() sites, the single biggest file in the 103-site count, and apps/refarm/src/commands/doctor.ts carries three more. This is the first time that cluster has been tied to a WRONG ANSWER rather than to a shape count, which is the entire reason this slice measures by consequence.

DO NOT CONFLATE THE COMPANION: 'refarm package-manager --json' is declared scope PROJECT in the probe and legitimately varies (pnpm here, npm elsewhere) -- detecting THIS tree's package manager is its job. The defect is doctor consuming that project fact and reporting it under a host.* name.

issues.title: plugin list reports the node's own plugin as unresolved from any other directory
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field path: plugins.

MEASURED: from /home/s095407044/github/refarm the single installed plugin reports packageSource 'workspace' with packageDir '/home/s095407044/github/refarm/packages/agent'; from /tmp the SAME plugin reports packageSource 'unresolved' with packageDir null. Same id (@refarm/agent), same version (0.1.0), same source (bundled) -- only the provenance fields collapse.

WHY IT MATTERS: a plugin is installed into the NODE's sovereign dir, and 'plugin status' (which reports what the daemon has LOADED) is correctly identical from all three directories. So the node knows perfectly well where its plugin came from; 'plugin list' re-derives that provenance from the caller's working tree instead of reading it. 'unresolved' is not a neutral word here -- it is what an operator sees before deciding whether a plugin is trustworthy, and it appears for a plugin that is fully resolved on the node.

This is the same family as the VPN defect the 2026-08-07 slice closed: node state presented through a working-tree lens, correct exactly where it is developed and wrong everywhere the operator actually stands. apps/refarm/src/commands/plugin-shared.ts carries 2 bare process.cwd() sites; audit before substituting, because resolving a WORKSPACE package legitimately needs a workspace root.

issues.title: surface list reads the caller's directory .refarm/config.json instead of the node's
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field paths: configPath, root, surfaces.

MEASURED: from the repository, root '/home/s095407044/github/refarm', configPath '/home/s095407044/github/refarm/.refarm/config.json', 3 surfaces. From /tmp, root '/tmp', configPath '/tmp/.refarm/config.json', 0 surfaces.

THIS IS THE FIXTURE DEFECT, EXACTLY AS THE 2026-08-07 SLICE NAMED IT. That slice found ovpn-serpro visible only from this checkout and recorded the finding in these words: 'visible from the repo, invisible everywhere else was never the feature working -- it was the SYMPTOM, the CLI reading a fixture and presenting it as the node's catalog.' The repo's .refarm/config.json is a gitignored dev fixture written while building that very feature. surface list is still reading it and presenting its three surfaces as the node's.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR DAILY USE: surfaces are how the operator reaches this node from Termux, the PWA and Telegram. A surface catalog that empties when he runs the command from anywhere but one checkout is the difference between 'my node offers three ways in' and 'my node offers none', decided by his shell's working directory. The honest empty answer -- 0 surfaces from every directory -- would at least be legible; 3-here and 0-there is the state that reads as working.

apps/refarm/src/commands/surface.ts carries 3 bare process.cwd() sites. The fix is the same one connection.ts took in d8f850b8: resolve declaredBase() rather than the caller's directory.

issues.title: Twenty-one read-only commands are probeable and not yet probed, held under a ratchet
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 while building the coverage test. The CLI has 187 leaf commands, not the 64 top-level ones the first count reported, and 181 of them accept --json -- the flag is nearly universal here. Of those, 64 require a positional argument the probe has no fixture for and are excluded by a DERIVED rule, 35 are probed, and 85 needed a decision.

Of the 85, twenty-one are read-only candidates that SHOULD be probed and have not been given a scope and a written reason yet: agent doctor, auth list, config plugins list, hardening, health audit, health policy, health suggest-policy, issues validate, model doctor, model env, process status, project automations list, project automations validate, provision list, records analyze, release check, release plan, workspace execution, workspace mounts, workspace sources declarations, workspace status.

They are NOT in the probe yet for one reason, and it is the ISS-091 lesson: `refarm task list` looked read-only from every angle a reviewer has -- it is called list, it prints, it exits 0 -- and it rewrites the node's task-session file on every read. Admitting twenty-one commands to an instrument that runs each of them four times per invocation, on the strength of their names, would repeat that mistake twenty-one times. Each needs the same treatment the 35 got: verify it writes nothing, decide node or project, write the reason.

THE BACKLOG IS RATCHETED, NOT MERELY LISTED. scripts/directory-independence-exclusions.mjs exports NOT_YET_PROBED_CEILING = 21 and apps/refarm/test/commands/probe-coverage.test.ts fails if the count exceeds it -- same discipline as no-os-resolution.mjs's BASELINE_MAX_OFFENDING_SITES. A new command may be excluded as mutating, interactive or expensive; it may not join this backlog. Lower the ceiling in the same commit that graduates a command into PROBE_COMMANDS.

Probing all 21 would raise the measured surface from 35 to 56 of the 116 commands that are probeable in principle (181 with --json, minus 64 needing arguments, minus the mutating and interactive ones).

issues.title: The directory-independence probe has no CI home until a seeded node fixture exists
issues.body:
DECISION 2026-08-10, taken from measurement rather than from the plan, which had said CI would run a subset of the probe and report its coverage as a fraction.

MEASURED under an empty REFARM_HOME, which is what CI has: `workspace list` returns [] from every directory and scores `same`; `connection status` does the same. `plugin list` and `surface list` still differ, because they read the WORKING TREE rather than the node's catalog.

So a CI run would catch two of the four real convictions and report agreement between two ABSENCES as `same` for the rest. A step that passes because it measured nothing is precisely the defect this instrument exists to find, and putting it in CI would have manufactured that defect inside the instrument.

WHAT IS TRUE INSTEAD: the probe is a local instrument run against a real node, and the tool now prints the caveat on every run rather than leaving it in a spec -- 'a verdict is only as strong as the node it was taken on'. The CI-side guard is apps/refarm/test/commands/probe-coverage.test.ts, which is pure, needs no node, and protects what CI can actually protect: that a new leaf command cannot join the CLI without being probed or excluded with a written reason.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS: a seeded node fixture in CI -- a declared catalog with at least two workspaces and a reachable daemon -- would make `same` mean agreement between two POPULATED answers instead of between two empty ones. At that point the probe becomes meaningful in CI and this item is the place to reopen the decision. Until then, running it there would buy a green that overclaims, which costs more than the coverage is worth.

issues.title: The probe records a non-zero exit as unrunnable, even when the command answered in JSON
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-10 while re-baselining the probe against the real second workspace. runCliFromDirectory treats ANY non-zero exit as unrunnable(...), so a command that answered with valid JSON and a negative verdict is recorded as one that did not run.

MEASURED: `refarm health --json` from ~/git/rcdc5/rcdc5 prints a complete envelope -- ok:false, issueCount 25, full results -- and exits non-zero. The probe reports it `unrunnable in: workspace:rcdc5`. It ran. It answered. The answer was 'this project has 25 health issues'.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: the two states are acted on differently. `unrunnable-somewhere` convicts a node-scoped command on the grounds that it refuses in some directories -- the ENOENT shape. A command that ANSWERS ok:false in one directory and ok:true in another is a different finding entirely, and one the probe should compare field by field rather than collapse into 'did not run'. Today a node command that started returning ok:false in one directory would be convicted for the right outcome with the wrong reason, and the diverging fields -- the actual evidence -- would be discarded.

FIX SHAPE: parse stdout first. If it is valid JSON, the command RAN, whatever its exit code, and the exit code itself becomes a compared value so a directory-dependent exit code is its own divergence rather than a lost fact. Reserve unrunnable for the cases that genuinely produced no comparable answer: a crash, a timeout, non-JSON stdout, a missing binary.

NOT FIXED IN THE SLICE THAT FOUND IT, deliberately: ISS-092's burn-down was the operator's instruction, `refarm resume` exits 0 from every directory, and this defect changes no verdict that ISS-092's proof depends on. It does change two rows -- `health` and `check --next-action` would move from unrunnable-somewhere to differs-undeclared, both still passing as project-scoped -- so it must land in its own commit with its own before/after table, not inside a fix that would then be crediting itself with someone else's change.

issues.title: doctor's advice fields still vary by directory: part by design, part ISS-094's symptom
issues.body:
RESIDUAL CONVICTION after ISS-093's fix, and the hypothesis this item was filed with was WRONG. Recorded here rather than left standing, using the writer ISS-085 built precisely so a body can be corrected without hand-editing a governed document.

FILED SAYING: sovereign:plugin-unknown fires only from /tmp and is almost certainly ISS-094's root cause -- plugin provenance re-derived from the caller's working tree.

MEASURED AFTER ISS-094 LANDED: it still fires. It comes from context.ts's built-plugin comparison, which reports null rather than trusting a fallback root when the invocation directory has no build. It is the same working-tree fact already declared as legitimate on the `context` probe row, and it has nothing to do with plugin list.

SO ALL SEVEN advice fields -- nextAction, nextActions, nextCommand, nextCommands, recommendations, warnings, warningCount -- trace to comparisons that are doctor's JOB: the scope:* findings come from doctor.ts:380's operatorBase, a deliberate cwd read the 2026-08-06 two-halves-one-node slice installed so the node could be compared against where the operator is standing, and a doctor whose scope findings did not move with the directory would have stopped doing the comparison at all.

RESOLVED by declaring them in scripts/directory-independence.mjs with a written reason per field, AFTER each was traced. The order matters and is the point: trace first, declare second. Declaring all seven while still believing one of them was another item's defect would have bought a green row by hiding a real finding, which is the 'fix by declaring' the burn-down's own rules forbid.

issues.title: Three doctor tests fail on a clean checkout because they read the real environment
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 by stashing every uncommitted change and running the suite against the committed HEAD: `pnpm --filter refarm exec vitest run test/commands/doctor.test.ts` reports 3 failed | 17 passed. The three are 'emits the first blocking recovery action as JSON', 'emits the first executable recovery command as JSON' and 'createDoctorCommand reports no connection findings when loadConfig throws'.

CAUSE: they drive createDoctorCommand against the REAL environment, and this checkout has a gitignored .refarm/ directory. That produces scope:auth-policy-divergence, context:home-divergence and sovereign:unloaded-dir findings, and the fixtures expect a nextActions list without them. The tests are not wrong about doctor; they are coupled to the machine they run on.

HOW IT STAYED INVISIBLE: `refarm agent finish --lane after-edit` passes, because the lane selects tests by change detection and these had not been touched. Two quality gates with different scopes is a known property of this repo, not a surprise -- but it means a green lane is not evidence that the suite is green.

IT IS NOT THIS SLICE'S DOING, and that is why it is filed rather than fixed inside another commit: the failures reproduce with zero of ISS-093's changes applied. Fixing them means injecting the scope comparison in those three tests the way the other doctor tests already do, so the fixture stops depending on whether the machine running it happens to have a .refarm/ beside the checkout.

issues.title: The probe's control pair is probabilistic: a field that moves only sometimes is excluded only sometimes
issues.body:
MY OWN DEFECT, found by the instrument turning on me. The control pair added on 2026-08-10 runs each command a second time in the first directory and excludes any field that differs between those two runs as time-variant. It works when the field MOVES during that pair -- and environmentPressure.signals, a live memory and free-space reading, sometimes does not move between two spawns seconds apart.

OBSERVED: the row `resume --workspace <self>` reported `same` on one run and `differs-undeclared` on the next, with no code change between them. A verdict that flips is worse than a verdict that is wrong, because nobody can tell which run to believe.

AND THE CONTROL COULD NEVER HAVE CAUGHT THE OTHER HALF: environmentPressure.signals carries the free space of the filesystem the command was invoked on (signals[].path is the cwd), so it varies by DIRECTORY too. A same-directory control is blind to that by construction. It is now declared with a written reason on both resume rows, which is the right answer for a field that varies for two independent causes.

WHAT REMAINS TO DECIDE, and it is a real design question rather than a bug to squash: the control pair is a PROBABILISTIC instrument sold as a measurement. Options, none free: run the pair in every directory instead of only the first (three chances instead of one, 50% more spawns, still probabilistic); run the pair N times (linear cost for asymptotic confidence); or accept that known-volatile fields are DECLARED and keep the control only as a safety net that catches new ones. The third is closest to how the rest of this instrument already works -- declarations carry written reasons and are counted apart from `same` -- but it gives up the self-expiring property that made the control attractive: a declaration outlives its reason, a measurement does not.

DO NOT close this by making the control run more times without saying so in the report. A probe that is 95% reliable and presents itself as 100% is the exact defect class this whole line of work exists to find.

issues.title: config.ts and the composition resolver anchor the user tier on the OS home, together
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-10 while closing ISS-050, and it is the reason that fix stopped where it did.

apps/refarm/src/utils/composition-resolver.ts's user tier MUST land on the exact file config.ts writes -- os.homedir()/.refarm/config.json -- so scalars and plugins[] share one file at every tier. Its header comment says so and calls it the CO-HABITATION GUARANTEE. Passing the REFARM_HOME-aware dirname(resolveRefarmHome()) would split the two into different files under a custom REFARM_HOME.

WHAT THAT ACTUALLY MEANS, said plainly: config.ts's user tier ALSO ignores REFARM_HOME. Under a declared home -- a sandbox node, a second device, anything the sovereign-state work exists to make possible -- both sides answer the operator's OS home. They are not correct; they are consistently WRONG TOGETHER, and the co-habitation guarantee is what keeps them consistent.

So the honest state after ISS-050 is: the silent default is gone (a caller that means the OS home now says so through a named cohabitationHome(), and the three plugin-install sites that were writing the working tree's agent.wasm into the operator's real ~/.refarm/assets/ now pass the DECLARED base), and this pair is left as it was, deliberately, because moving one without the other would split a file the composition layer depends on being single.

TO CLOSE THIS: config.ts's user tier and the composition resolver's user tier move to the declared base TOGETHER, in one change, with a test that pins them to the same path under a custom REFARM_HOME. Anything less either splits the file or leaves the pair anchored to a home the node did not declare. It is a small change and a scary one, which is why it is filed rather than smuggled into a slice about something else.

issues.title: An env injected through deps stops at loadConfig, which reads process.env directly
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 by stashing every uncommitted change and running the file against the committed HEAD: `vitest run src/commands/workspace-sync.test.ts` reported 9 failed | 10 passed, all nine with MissingSovereignDirError.

CAUSE, and it is a plumbing gap rather than a test mistake: the tests DO inject their environment -- `runWorkspaceSync({...}, { root, env: { SOVEREIGN_DIR: '.refarm' } })` -- and that env never reaches `loadConfig`, which reads `process.env` for the sovereign-dir selector through sovereignConfigPathCandidates. `loadConfig(root, options)` takes an options bag and has no `env` in it. So the injection is honoured by the code the test can see and ignored by the code it cannot.

WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the CLI sets SOVEREIGN_DIR in-process, so the daemon and every real invocation are fine; only a test harness that constructs the call directly hits it. And the after-edit lane selects tests by change detection, so a file nobody touched is a file nobody runs -- the same reason ISS-100's three doctor tests sat failing.

UNBLOCKED FOR NOW, not fixed: the test file pins process.env.SOVEREIGN_DIR in beforeAll and restores it in afterAll, with a comment naming this item. That makes the file state its own environment instead of inheriting one, which is the ISS-100 shape, but it leaves the real gap standing: an env injected through deps stops at the first module that reads process.env directly.

TO CLOSE: `loadConfig` accepts `{ env }` and threads it to sovereignDir/sovereignConfigPathCandidates, and the call sites that already carry an operator env pass it. That is a small change with a wide blast radius -- loadConfig is called from nearly every command -- so it wants its own slice and a test that proves an injected env reaches the path resolution, rather than being folded into a workspace-sync change.

issues.title: refarm agent doctor dispatches a prompt and writes five files, including the graph
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 while graduating commands out of the not-yet-probed backlog (ISS-096), using the read-only observation ISS-091 left behind. Of twenty candidates, nineteen touched nothing. `refarm agent doctor --json` touched FIVE files on the operator's real node in a single run:

  ~/.refarm/data/refarm/default.db
  ~/.refarm/scarecrow-audit.ndjson
  ~/.refarm/streams/activity.ndjson
  ~/.refarm/streams/urn:tractor:stream:response:urn:sovereign:prompt-<uuid>.ndjson
  ~/.refarm/task-results/<uuid>.json

A stream named `response:...prompt-<uuid>` and a task-result file are not diagnostics. This command DISPATCHES: it runs a prompt through the agent and writes the effort's whole trail. It took 2.1 seconds where every other candidate took 0.4.

WHY THAT IS WORSE THAN ISS-091'S `task list`: a write to a session file is tidiness. This one creates a graph record, an audit entry, a stream and a result -- and, depending on the route, spends the operator's paid model quota. `agent doctor` reads as the safest thing in the CLI: it is the command you run to ASK WHETHER THE AGENT IS OK, and an operator debugging a broken node will run it repeatedly.

IT WAS ALSO ABOUT TO BE ADMITTED TO AN INSTRUMENT THAT RUNS EVERY PROBED COMMAND FOUR TIMES PER PASS. It is excluded under `mutates` and stays out until this is decided.

TO DECIDE, and it is the operator's rather than mine: does `agent doctor` mean 'is the agent reachable and configured' (a read, and then the dispatch belongs behind a flag or a separate verb), or does it mean 'prove the agent answers' (a dispatch, and then the NAME is the problem, and its cost and quota use should be stated before it runs)? Either is defensible; what is not defensible is a command that looks like the first and does the second.

issues.title: Eight runtime tests fail on a clean checkout — the third file with environment-coupled tests
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10: 8 failed on a clean checkout, environment-coupled — the third file in one session with the same defect (doctor.test.ts, workspace-sync.test.ts, runtime.test.ts).

CLOSED 2026-08-11, and NOT by touching this file. The cause was the one ISS-109 names: the throwaway-HOME containment lived in apps/refarm/vitest.setup.ts alone, and change detection meant a file nobody touched was a file nobody ran, so these sat failing against the operator machine that wrote them.

Moving that containment into @refarm.dev/vtconfig baseConfig.test.setupFiles — so every workspace inherits it and no resolvable config can lack it — fixed these eight without a line changing in runtime.test.ts.

  pnpm -C apps/refarm exec vitest run test/commands/runtime.test.ts
  Tests  32 passed (32)

The pattern this item named was right and the fix belonged one level up: a test that reads process.env or the real filesystem passes on the machine that wrote it and fails everywhere else, and no per-file repair addresses that. The lane gap it also named is closed separately (ISS-107: after-edit now runs the affected package tests).

issues.title: scripts/ is the repo's 2nd largest surface and 70% of it has no test
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10, not estimated:

  scripts/ (production)  185 files  42,340 lines   <- 2nd largest surface after apps/refarm/src (65,280)
    with test:   54 (29%)  19,773 lines
    WITHOUT:    131 (70%)  22,567 lines

For scale: packages/toolbox/src is 3,001 lines. scripts/ is 14x it, and larger than every package.

scripts/repo-complexity-check.mjs gates only FILE LENGTH (DEFAULT_MAX_COMPLEXITY_LINES = 1000).
Nothing gates the untested fraction, so it can only grow.

THE OTHER HALF, measured 2026-08-11 and worse than the first: THE 30% THAT DOES HAVE TESTS IS
NEVER RUN BY ANY LANE.

package.json registers roughly NINETY `node --test` entries -- `no-os-resolution:test`,
`directory-independence:test`, `refarm:sandbox:test`, `project:validate:test`, and on -- each
individually invocable and none of them reached by `refarm agent finish` in any lane. The lanes
run vitest through turbo, which does not see `node --test` scripts at all.

PROVEN BY ACCIDENT, which is the only reason it was noticed: `scripts/no-os-resolution.test.mjs`
sat RED for hours on 2026-08-11. The commit that split `declared-base.js` out of config's barrel
added a third module to ALLOWLISTED_RESOLVER_MODULES, and the test pins that list BY VALUE. Every
lane stayed green -- after-edit, after-commit, and a full `turbo run test` across 282 tasks --
because none of them runs that file. It surfaced only when a later slice ran it by hand.

  All nine top-level scripts/*.test.mjs suites, run by hand: 288 assertions, all passing.
  Reached by the agent cadence: zero.

SO THERE ARE TWO GAPS, and they want different fixes:

  1. 70% of scripts/ has no test. A ceiling on the untested count, same three-counter form as
     scripts/no-os-resolution.mjs (total / burn-down / always-zero), delta 0.
  2. The tests that DO exist are unreachable from the cadence. This one is cheaper and worth
     more: an aggregate script (`pnpm run scripts:test`) that runs every `scripts/**/*.test.mjs`,
     plus a lane step. Without it, gap 1's ceiling would guard tests nothing ever runs.

Do (2) first. A test nobody runs is not coverage; it is a file that agrees with itself.

WHAT NOT TO DO YET: the three largest scripts are the ones still moving -- refarm-sandbox.mjs
(2,209 LOC, 17 commits/90d), directory-independence.mjs (1,189 / 14), vault-seed-ready-handoff.mjs
(923 / 28). Freezing an interface under churn is the failure mode CLAUDE.md section 3 warns about.

THE GRADUATION CRITERION, from the one precedent that worked: reso graduated to packages/toolbox
(leaving a deprecated wrapper) because agents run it every slice -- a script earns the toolbox
when it becomes a VERB somebody types repeatedly, not when it gets big.

issues.title: No agent finish lane runs the test suite: a broken test passes after-edit AND before-push
issues.body:
PROVEN 2026-08-11 by poisoning a real test and running the real gates, not by reading the code.

A deliberately broken assertion in packages/config/src/config-tiers.test.js:

  pnpm --filter @refarm.dev/config run test   ->  Tests  1 failed | 142 passed (143)
  refarm agent finish --lane after-edit  --run --json  ->  ok: true
  refarm agent finish --lane before-push --run --json  ->  ok: true

Both lanes green. The test suite red.

WHAT EACH LANE ACTUALLY RUNS (refarm agent finish --lane X --json, 2026-08-11):

  after-edit    tidy imports --check ; check --next-action
  after-commit  + turbo lint --filter=<changed package>
  handoffs      + pnpm -C apps/refarm run test:handoffs
  before-push   + turbo type-check lint build (apps/refarm, packages/cli, storage-fs,
                  barn, config) ; validate-packages ; task:build-order:check ;
                  scripts/security/audit.mjs

NO LANE RUNS `turbo run test`. The `test` task EXISTS in turbo.json with
dependsOn: ['build'] -- it is defined and never invoked by the agent loop. The only
test execution anywhere in the cadence is `test:handoffs`, which is one narrow suite
in one app.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING STEP: CLAUDE.md section 4 prescribes these lanes as
THE operator loop, in the imperative ("After source edits, before committing: refarm
agent finish --lane after-edit --run --json"). An agent following the documented cadence
exactly -- all four lanes, every gate green -- can commit and push a broken test suite.
The cadence is the quality instrument this repo asks agents to trust instead of asking
the operator to eyeball diffs. It currently does not measure the thing it is trusted for.

FOUND BY ACCIDENT, which is itself the evidence: while adding config-tiers.test.js I used
node:test in a package that runs vitest. The file had ZERO tests ("No test suite found")
and the package test script exited 1. `after-edit` reported ok: true. If I had not run the
package test by hand out of habit, a test file that ran nothing would have been committed
under a green gate.

WHAT TO DECIDE (operator): whether after-edit runs the CHANGED package's tests (fast,
scoped, the same --filter shape after-commit already uses for lint) or whether tests join
before-push only (slower feedback, cheaper per-edit). The lanes already know how to scope
by changed package -- after-commit's lint step proves the mechanism exists and works.

RELATED: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-07-who-owns-this-work.md and the before-push
memory entry both record that this lane was audited and extended (scaffold, build order,
audit). Tests were not part of that audit, so the lane is trusted for a property nobody
checked it had.

issues.title: Four order-dependent test failures in apps/refarm, now visible because after-edit runs tests
issues.body:
Surfaced by ISS-107's fix: after-edit now runs the affected package's tests.

CORRECTION, 2026-08-11 — the original body of this item claimed the failures were ORDER-DEPENDENT,
citing a filtered run reporting a different set than a full one. That was wrong, and the error was
mine: `pnpm --filter <pkg> exec vitest` executes from the REPO ROOT, so those runs resolved the
root vitest.config.js and never loaded apps/refarm's own config or setup file. Two different
configs, not two different orderings. Under the correct invocation (`pnpm -C apps/refarm`, which is
what turbo and the package's own `test` script use) the failing set is stable at four. The same
mistake also inflated the colour measurement quoted in ISS-107's commit; re-measured correctly, it
is 11 colour failures -> 0, not 5 -> 16.

THE FOUR, and none was what the original body guessed:

1. workspace.test.ts x2 -- STALE, and stale because the code got BETTER. `nodeCatalogPath` now
   returns an ABSOLUTE path and documents why: a bare ".refarm/config.json" reads as the
   workspace's OWN file, which `localWorkspaceDeclarationAbolishedMessage` refuses outright ("a
   workspace never declares itself or another workspace, in any file"). The test was asserting the
   string the code forbids. The `instructions` array had likewise GAINED the line stating that very
   rule, and the test's verbatim copy of the old three strings failed for it. Fixed by pinning the
   RULES (the no-self-declaration sentence, the next command, `ref null`) instead of the prose.

2. process-boundary.test.ts -- NOT a stale test. A real architecture violation:
   sovereign-divergence-doctor.ts:140 hardcoded `command: "refarm context --json"` instead of
   building it through `refarmCommand([...])`. The binary's name comes from the environment
   (ADR-087: a white-label build supplies it). The guard was right and had one live offender.

3. surface.test.ts -- the same lesson the Rust `CwdGuard` taught one commit earlier, in
   TypeScript. The test did `process.chdir(root)` and expected `surface list` to follow. It does
   not, and rightly: surfaces are how the NODE exposes itself, so it resolves from
   `declaredBase()`. Once the suite gained a throwaway HOME, `declaredBase()` correctly stopped
   following the cwd and the assertion broke -- the test was pinning the behaviour this whole
   burn-down exists to remove. It DECLARES its base now (SOVEREIGN_BASE) instead of walking into
   a directory.

Result: apps/refarm 3269 passed, 0 failed (220 files).

COST OF THE WRONG INVOCATION, recorded because it was not free: the full root-config run wrote to
the operator's real machine -- see the sibling item on the containment bypass.

issues.title: pnpm --filter exec runs from the repo root, bypassing a package's test containment (it wrote to the operator's live config)
issues.body:
RESOLVED 2026-08-11. Both halves shipped, and the second one is the fix this item asked for.

WHAT HAPPENED (unchanged): `pnpm --filter <pkg> exec <cmd>` runs from the REPO ROOT, unlike
`--filter <pkg> run <script>` and `pnpm -C <pkg> exec`. So `pnpm --filter refarm exec vitest run`
resolved the root vitest.config.js, which loads no package setup file. apps/refarm's containment
-- throwaway HOME plus an fs write guard -- never ran. Proven with a probe: `setup 0ms`, HOME was
the operator's real home, and a writeFileSync into it succeeded with no guard error.

DAMAGE, repaired the same session: `spawnEnv` deleted from the live ~/.refarm/config.json (the
PATH/HOME the Rust host injects into every spawned process, restored verbatim from
config.json.bak-20260809005833), a fixture plugin id written into `trusted_plugins`, four
`revokedPlugins*` keys added, and escape.txt / refarm-guard-fixture-escape.txt ("this must never
land on disk") / refarm-support.json dropped in the working tree. `refarm check` back to ok.
Pre-repair state kept at ~/.refarm/config.json.bak-antes-do-reparo-20260811.

FIX 1 -- the root config REFUSES. vitest.config.js excludes every apps/* and packages/*
directory that owns a vitest config, computed at load time so a package gaining one is covered
the day it does. The dangerous invocation exits 1 with "No test files found".

FIX 2 -- the containment becomes INHERITED, which is what this item said was still open.
packages/vtconfig/src/home-containment.js is now baseConfig.test.setupFiles, so all 64 workspaces
get the throwaway HOME/USERPROFILE/REFARM_HOME/XDG_*/SOVEREIGN_BASE/SOVEREIGN_DIR before any test
file's imports run. No resolvable config can lack it.

MEASURED, not assumed: `turbo run test` across the whole monorepo, 257 of 264 tasks successful.
The one failing package (@refarm.dev/farmhand, 2 of 232) was verified NOT to be the containment
by stashing it and re-running -- 2 failed either way, stale hardcoded model defaults, fixed in the
same commit. The shared containment broke ZERO tests across 64 packages.

DELIBERATELY NOT MOVED, and the reason is a measurement: the fs WRITE GUARD stays package-local.
Layer 0 redirects and forbids nothing; the write guard THROWS outside the sandbox, and 101 test
files in this monorepo write through writeFileSync/mkdirSync. Turning a throw on for 64
workspaces in one move is rewriting the suite, not containing it. Adoption package by package is
tracked separately.

STILL WORTH DOING (not blocking): CLAUDE.md section 3 already prescribes
`pnpm --filter <pkg> run <script>` and is right; a sentence naming `exec` as the trap would help,
since the two read as siblings and behave differently. Held rather than written, per the
operator's standing rule that CLAUDE.md takes only long-term content.

issues.title: Adopt the fs write guard package by package (Layer 1 of the test containment)
issues.body:
Split out of ISS-109 with a measurement, not a hunch.

ISS-109 moved LAYER 0 -- the throwaway HOME -- into @refarm.dev/vtconfig's baseConfig, so all 64
workspaces inherit it. It broke zero tests, because it REDIRECTS: it relocates where a resolver
lands and forbids nothing.

LAYER 1 is the fs write guard in apps/refarm/vitest.setup.ts. It REFUSES: every mutating fs entry
point (writeFile, mkdir, rm, rename, open, createWriteStream, ... in both callback and Sync form)
throws a SandboxEscape when the target resolves outside the OS temp dir. That is the layer that
turns "a test wrote somewhere it should not" from a silent fact into a failing test naming the
path and the test.

WHY IT WAS NOT MOVED WITH LAYER 0:

  101 test files in this monorepo write through writeFileSync/mkdirSync.
  138 use tmpdir() and are already compatible.

Switching a throw on for 64 workspaces in one move would be rewriting the suite, not containing
it. The right shape is adoption package by package, each one measured.

THE ADOPTION, per package:
  1. Add the guard to that package's setup (or opt in via a shared helper exported from
     vtconfig -- worth extracting once the second adopter exists, not before).
  2. Run that package's suite. Every SandboxEscape is a real finding: either the test writes
     outside tmp (fix the test) or the CODE does (fix the code, and that one is the valuable
     case -- it is the class that deleted `spawnEnv` from the operator's live config).
  3. Record the count in the commit message so the next package knows what it is buying.

WHY IT IS WORTH THE WORK AT ALL, in one sentence: Layer 0 makes a stray write land somewhere
harmless; Layer 1 makes it land nowhere and say so. Only the second one finds the bug.

DO NOT do this as one sweeping change. The whole reason ISS-109 exists is that containment which
one config can fail to load is a convention, and the fix for that is not a bigger sweep -- it is
a floor everything inherits (done) plus a stricter tier packages opt into knowingly (this).

issues.title: projectResolution.cwd rides on a flag-origin resolution, where the directory played no part
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-11 by the seeded-node fixture (ISS-097) on its first run, and not by any probe run
against the operator's own node -- which is the argument for having the fixture.

`refarm resume --workspace <id> --json` from three directories:

  state       absent                      identical
  reason      no-handoff-in-workspace     identical
  workspaceId <id>                        identical
  declared    ["alpha","beta"]            identical
  projectResolution.cwd                   VARIES

The guarantee holds: an explicitly named workspace is a node-level address and the ANSWER does
not move. What moves is a diagnostic about the question.

THE QUESTION: does `cwd` belong in a resolution whose origin is `flag` at all?

  - When the origin is `cwd-match` or `cwd-convention`, `cwd` is HOW the answer was reached and
    reporting it is the point -- ISS-092 added the whole `projectResolution` block so a consumer
    could see which of four states produced the project block and why.
  - When the origin is `flag`, the operator named the workspace. The current directory played no
    part in the resolution, and including it makes an otherwise directory-independent answer
    vary. A consumer diffing two `resume --workspace X` payloads across machines sees a
    difference that means nothing.

WHY IT IS ONLY VISIBLE UNDER THE FIXTURE: on a populated node the named workspace HAS a
.project/handoff.json, so the state is `read` and this branch never runs. The fixture reaches
the `absent` branch a real node cannot -- `state: absent, reason: no-handoff-in-workspace`.

FILED, NOT FIXED, and deliberately: removing a field from a `--json` payload is a contract
change, and it arrived inside a slice about the probe's CI home. The variance is declared in
`scripts/directory-independence.mjs` with this reasoning attached, so the probe reports it
rather than convicting it, and the declaration is where a future reader will find the question.

IF TAKEN UP: the smallest honest version is to omit `cwd` when `from === "flag"`, the same
absent-not-null rule the rest of that payload already follows (a key the caller did not
influence carries no key at all). Check `apps/refarm/src/commands/resume.ts`'s
`resolveProjectHandoff` and the tests that pin `projectResolution`.

issues.title: TASK_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_SCHEMA is declared twice with different values — one name, two wire contracts
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-11 while repairing the fifteen script suites (ISS-106). `TASK_ARTIFACT_MANIFEST_SCHEMA`
is declared TWICE, with DIFFERENT values:

  scripts/ci/check-task-artifact-manifests.mjs:6   "refarm.task-artifacts.v1"
  packages/artifact-contract-v1/src/types.ts:2     "sovereign.task-artifacts.v1"

One name, two wire contracts. A reader who greps the constant finds whichever copy is nearer.

HOW IT HAPPENED: ADR-087 phase 3 debranded the generic packages, so the package constant became
`sovereign.*`. `scripts/ci/` is NOT a brand-free surface -- `release:brand:guard` polices
`packages/`, not scripts -- so nothing forced the CI copy to move, and nothing noticed it had not.

A THIRD CONSUMER already picks a side by hand: scripts/ci/local-first-platform-proof.mjs:70 tests
`manifest?.schema === "refarm.task-artifacts.v1"` as a literal. So a manifest produced through the
PACKAGE would fail that check today.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY EMITTED, measured through requirements-supply-composition:
  result.schema                     refarm.requirements-supply-composition.v1   (the CI envelope)
  result.artifacts.reviewReport     refarm.requirements-supply-review.v1        (the CI envelope)
  result.artifacts.manifest         sovereign.task-artifacts.v1                 (from the package)

So one payload carries both prefixes. That is not wrong on its face -- an envelope may legitimately
carry a foreign schema -- but the DUPLICATE CONSTANT is, and the literal in local-first is a bug
waiting for the producer to change.

WHY IT IS FILED AND NOT FIXED: a wire name is a contract. Renaming the CI copy to `sovereign.*`
would change what a consumer reads off disk, and choosing which of the two names is canonical
inside a slice about repairing tests would be deciding it by accident. The three call sites are
listed above so whoever takes it does not have to find them again.

THE SMALLEST HONEST FIX, if taken up: scripts/ci/check-task-artifact-manifests.mjs imports the
constant from @refarm.dev/artifact-contract-v1 instead of declaring its own, and
local-first-platform-proof.mjs compares against the imported constant instead of a literal. That
makes the package the single declaration and leaves the VALUE decision (which prefix) as the one
question to answer.

RELATED: `check:permission-vocab` and `check:config-node-keys` are this repo's existing idiom for
pinning a vocabulary across two stacks. A third guard of that shape would catch the next duplicate
constant by construction rather than by someone repairing a test.

issues.title: content-projection joined the requirements-supply profile with no consumer proof, blocking the handoff
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-11 by `requirements:supply:handoff:test`, one of the fifteen script suites no lane
ran (ISS-106). The gate is right; the config has a gap.

  requirements-supply-handoff: blocked
    @refarm.dev/content-projection  missing consumer-proven tag
    @refarm.dev/content-projection  does not declare requirements-supply consumer proof metadata

  consumer-proven, correctly: @refarm.dev/enrichment-contract-v1,
                              @refarm.dev/records-contract-v1,
                              @refarm.dev/source-web

`@refarm.dev/content-projection` is a member of the `requirements-supply` profile in
refarm.config.json and carries neither the `consumer-proven` tag nor the consumer-proof metadata
the other three carry. So the whole handoff reports `ok: false` and the lane cannot promote.

WHY THIS WAS NOT FIXED IN THE SLICE THAT FOUND IT: adding the tag is not a code change, it is a
CLAIM -- that a consumer has pulled this package and proved it works. Nobody has verified that,
and stamping it to turn a test green is manufacturing exactly the evidence the gate exists to
demand. The test was updated to assert the honest state instead, naming this package as the
blocker, so the day the claim becomes true the test fails and gets updated deliberately.

THE OPERATOR DECIDES WHICH IS TRUE:
  a) content-projection HAS been consumer-proven -> add the tag and the `consumerPull` metadata
     (proofId / downstreamUse / proofTarget / ownershipBoundary, the four fields
     test-release-boundary-audit.mjs requires of every vault-seed-ready profile).
  b) It has NOT -> it does not belong in the `requirements-supply` profile yet, and removing the
     tag is the honest move until a consumer pulls it.

Either way the handoff goes green for a reason rather than by assertion. (a) is a claim to
verify; (b) is a scope correction.

issues.title: ADR-087 phase 3 unfinished: 21 brand literals in 10 generic packages
issues.body:
ADR-087 phase 3: a generic package never names the brand. A white-label build supplies the binary;
the package takes it.

MEASURED 2026-08-11 by `release:brand:guard`, one of the fifteen script suites no lane ran
(ISS-106): 21 literals across 10 packages. Now 6 across 4.

THE RULE THIS BURN-DOWN ESTABLISHED, written where it is enforced
(packages/process-systemd-user/src/unit.ts):

  A string PRINTED to the operator is a LABEL and takes the caller's binary.
  A string WRITTEN to disk, or matched against what is already there, is a VALUE and stays literal.

`UNIT_PREFIX = "refarm-"` is the canonical value: it lands on disk as `refarm-<name>.service` and
is how every ALREADY-INSTALLED unit is found again. Threading a binary into it would not debrand
anything -- it would rename units that exist and lose track of running processes.

CLOSED (15 of 21), and the four shapes they took:

  PARAMETERIZED (7). process-systemd-user + process-contract-v1: install advice, linger advice,
  lifetime description, bundled-consent refusal. `binary` is a REQUIRED, undefaulted option --
  the shape `buildCapabilities(binary)` already uses in @refarm.dev/cli. A default is what makes
  a brand literal survive a debranding, because nothing exercises it.

  DEFAULT REMOVED (1). `createLocalCaProvider`'s `caName` defaulted to the brand while all four
  call sites already passed it. Pure redundancy that happened to spell the brand; now required.

  FALLBACK NEUTRALIZED (4). `subjectCommonName` and `linuxCaAnchorPath` fell back to the brand
  when a label sanitized to nothing; `renderSystemdUnit`'s `generator`/`rewriteCommand` options
  ALREADY existed and only their defaults were branded. A caller that supplies nothing now gets a
  truthful string that names no tool, instead of the wrong one.

  INVENTION REMOVED (3). This is the best of the four. `operation-web-v1/wire.ts` and
  `farm-client/remote-initiation.mjs` fell back to `` `refarm ${id}` `` when the wire carried no
  command -- guessing a command line and presenting the guess as the operation's command. They
  return the ID ALONE now. The wire.ts test's own name asked for it: "reads the node-owned catalog
  without inventing missing ids". And `process-contract-v1`'s parser example teaches SHAPE (array,
  not shell line), so it names no binary at all rather than threading one through a pure parser.

REMAINING (6):

  cli/src/workspace-declaration.ts (3) -- NOT a defect. `WORKSPACE_KINDS` is
  ["refarm","consumer","lab","vault","project"]: the brand is a KIND ID in a vocabulary, and this
  file compares against it. Identical to `config/src/workspaces-config.js`, which the guard's own
  ALLOWLIST already carries with exactly that reason. This is an allowlist entry to write, not
  code to change -- and writing it is a deliberate act, so it is left for whoever agrees.

  std/src/bind-guard.ts, emoji-sas-v1/src/http.ts, farm-client/src/reach.mjs (3) -- advice strings
  in functions with no options bag. Each needs a signature to carry the binary, which is a
  contract change per package rather than a rename. farm-client is additionally ZERO-DEP and
  cannot import a resolver, though it already receives `env` (see its `declared-base.mjs` for the
  precedent).

  Until then `release:brand:guard` stays in run-script-tests.mjs's KNOWN_FAILING, whose entries
  carry their reason.

issues.title: GET /tasks and list_tasks both answer 'the newest N' and neither says by which clock
issues.body:
FILED 2026-08-11 while fixing ISS-041, as the half that fix deliberately did not close.

`GET /tasks` orders by `created_at_ns`. The guest's `list_tasks`
(packages/agent/src/tool_dispatch/task_tools.rs) goes through the bridge and gets the store's
`updated_at DESC, id DESC`. For any Task whose status changed since creation -- the ordinary case,
since a Task is created `active` and later becomes done/failed/blocked -- the two diverge. Same
data, same phrase "the newest N", two different answers.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE, and that is the second time it has been true in this family. The
plan said to drop the `created_at_ns` sort and let the store's order be the answer, which does make
them agree. It also silently changes what `refarm tasks` MEANS -- from "the newest tasks" to "the
most recently touched tasks" -- and makes it disagree with farmhand's own /tasks route, which sorts
by created_at_ns in TypeScript. Two surfaces agreeing on the wrong answer is not an improvement over
two surfaces answering different questions.

THE ACTUAL DEFECT is that neither surface says WHICH QUESTION IT ANSWERS. An operator listing tasks
reasonably wants the newest by creation; an agent loading prompt context reasonably wants the most
recently active. Both are defensible; neither is labelled. Same shape-versus-purpose distinction the
no-os-resolution ratchet needed before it could tell a defect from a legitimate site.

WAYS OUT, cheapest first:
  (a) name the order in each response (`order: "created" | "touched"`), change no behaviour, and let
      a caller that cares assert on it. Cheap, honest, and it makes future drift visible.
  (b) give the bridge an ordering parameter so `list_tasks` can ask for either. Touches the WIT
      surface and packages/agent.
  (c) pick one clock for both. Only correct if someone establishes that one question is right for
      all three consumers, which nobody has.

NOT URGENT: each is a correct answer to its own question and no consumer is known to break on the
difference. Filed so the next reader does not rediscover it as a bug.

issues.title: process add can be attended from another surface and process install cannot
issues.body:
FILED 2026-08-11 while installing the automation timer (ISS-066, path b).

`refarm process add` takes `--attended-elsewhere` -- "no terminal here, and that is fine, you are
attending from another surface". `refarm process install` takes no such flag, and its consent
channel is `process.stdin.isTTY`. So an operator away from a terminal CAN DECLARE A PROCESS AND
CANNOT INSTALL IT. The declaration lands, `refarm process status` reports "declared, but no unit is
installed", and the one command that closes the gap is the one that cannot be reached.

THE REFUSAL ITSELF IS RIGHT and must not be weakened. Its own comment says why: a consent prompt
with no operator behind it does not default to yes and does not default to no -- it never gets
asked. Building a stdio channel on a non-interactive stdin would make the command wait forever for
a decision nobody is there to make. Piping an answer in, or faking a TTY, forges an operator's
presence at a consent gate, which is the one thing this design exists to prevent.

WHAT IS MISSING IS THE OTHER SURFACE, not a bypass. This node can already ask a human a question on
whichever device they are holding -- the pending-prompt system works today and its own tests show
answers arriving from `my-phone` and `delivery:pocket`. `process add` reaches it via
`--attended-elsewhere`; `process install` does not reach it at all.

WAYS OUT, cheapest first:
  (a) give `process install` the same `--attended-elsewhere` path `process add` already has. The
      consent block takes a channel; this is about which channel gets built, not about weakening
      the gate.
  (b) let `refarm agent finish` / a handoff carry the pending decision, so an install proposed by a
      background session is waiting on the operator's phone rather than lost.

BLOCKS, concretely: an automation timer proposed by an agent cannot be turned on without the
operator sitting at this machine. Everything up to the install is reachable; the last inch is not.

CLOSED 2026-08-11 by path (a), and MEASURING CORRECTED THIS ITEM'S OWN MECHANISM TWICE.

First correction: the body above says the node "can already ask a human on whichever device they
are holding" and cites the tests. A first pass at confirming that found only tests calling
`setPromptPublisher` and concluded the phone path was library-only. That was wrong -- a `preAction`
hook in apps/refarm/src/program.ts installs the publisher on EVERY command via
`installDeclaredDelivery`. The path is live in production; `process install` simply never reached
it, because `resolveOperatorChannel` returned null on `!process.stdin.isTTY` before any channel was
built.

Second correction, and this one changed the implementation: `--attended-elsewhere` alone would NOT
have worked. `createStdioOperatorChannel` PEERS a terminal against the node's hub and lets whoever
answers first win. With no terminal that race is not useless, it is harmful: `readline` settles a
non-TTY stdin immediately -- a closed or piped input fires `close`, which becomes
`OperatorPromptCancelledError` -- so the local side rejects FIRST, wins, and the peered channel
withdraws the question from the phone before anyone could see it. It would have reported
"cancelled" for a question the operator was never shown, which is worse than the refusal it
replaced.

So the fix is a channel, not a flag: `createAttendedOperatorChannel` in
@refarm.dev/prompt-contract-v1 asks the publisher's remote side ALONE, and returns `null` when
nothing publishes -- a claim about a human is not a wire, and a claim with no wire behind it is
still nobody to ask.

PROVEN ON THIS NODE, not only in tests:

    refarm process install automations --attended-elsewhere --json < /dev/null
    -> GET /prompts on the sidecar shows 1 pending, asker {command: "refarm process install",
       host: "serpro-1577853", pid: ...}

Without the flag it still answers `no-operator`, unchanged.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, and the operator named it while this landed: it does not let an operation
GET HIS ATTENTION. The prompt lives exactly as long as the process that asked -- principle P1 in
packages/tractor/src/sidecar/pending_prompt.rs -- so a question published by a background run
vanishes when that run ends. Killing the probe above left zero pending prompts behind, correctly.
That is ISS-077's subject, and it is the difference between "he is already here, ask him" (this
item) and "reach him, wait for him to say he is attentive, then act" (still open).
issues.resolved_by: path (a): --attended-elsewhere on `process install`, backed by a remote-only operator channel

issues.title: --attended-elsewhere built a peered channel that cancelled the question it was meant to send
issues.body:
FOUND AND FIXED 2026-08-11, immediately after ISS-116 -- the same defect, in every other command
that offered the flag. Recorded because the FIX is a pattern the next such command must follow, and
because a one-line diff hides how the failure looked.

`--attended-elsewhere` means "no terminal here, and that is fine -- you are attending from another
surface". Five commands offered it: process add, process install, surface add, workspace sync,
workspace command add. Each gated its refusal on `atTerminal || attendedElsewhere` AND THEN BUILT
`createStdioOperatorChannel()` REGARDLESS OF WHICH ONE WAS TRUE.

That channel peers a terminal against the node's hub and lets whoever answers first win. Measured
against the real modules with stdin at /dev/null:

    the question is printed to a terminal nobody is reading
    the local side rejects        OperatorPromptCancelledError
    it WINS the race
    pending prompts on the hub: 0        <- withdrawn before any device could show it

So the flag did the OPPOSITE of what its help text promised, in every command that offered it. It
appeared to work only when something was actively writing to stdin -- a remote pty -- which is the
one case the flag was not needed for.

THE FIX IS A CHANNEL SELECTOR, `createOperatorChannelFor({ atTerminal, attendedElsewhere })`, which
picks by the same evidence the guard already weighed:
  at a terminal              -> peered (terminal AND devices; either answers, the other withdraws)
  attended, no terminal      -> the devices ALONE
  neither, or attended with nothing publishing -> null, and the caller REFUSES

THE NEAR-MISS IS THE PART WORTH READING. The first draft of this fix ended the workspace call sites
in `?? createAutoOperatorChannel()`. That channel returns each prompt's DEFAULT without asking --
`prompt.default ?? true` for a confirm -- so it would have AUTO-APPROVED the very operations the
guard exists to gate, silently, in the slice that was fixing consent. Caught before it shipped. A
null channel must refuse; it must never fall back to something that answers on the operator's
behalf.

NOT CHANGED, deliberately: `delivery test` builds the terminal channel directly. Its guard refuses
without a terminal on purpose -- "a real message would leave this machine" -- so there is no
attended-elsewhere path there to match.

issues.title: A question whose precondition already holds should not be asked, and one answer still lets N askers act
issues.body:
OPENED 2026-08-11 by the operator, while coalescing landed in the prompt hub. Coalescing solves
the half the hub owns; this is the half it cannot.

HIS CASE, in his words: an operator (or an agent) keeps asking to connect the VPN WHEN IT IS
ALREADY CONNECTED; and something that needs that connection should use the one that exists, or
wait for him to pay attention.

WHAT COALESCING NOW DOES: N askers declaring the same subject wait on ONE card, and one answer
settles all of them. That kills the duplicate cards and the "tap four times for one VPN".

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and must not be mistaken for: it does not know whether the VPN is ALREADY UP.
A question whose precondition is already satisfied should not be asked at all -- and after one
answer, N joined askers each proceed, so N of them may each try to connect. The hub settles
DECISIONS; it does not own the resource.

THE MISSING PRIMITIVE is a precondition the asker states and something checks, twice:
  1. BEFORE publishing -- if the state already holds, do not ask. An operator asked to authorise
     something already true learns that the questions are noise, which is how a consent surface
     stops working without ever going red.
  2. AFTER the answer, before acting -- the world may have changed while the card stood on a
     phone. This is the same lesson `truncated` taught: the gap between measuring and acting is
     where the wrong answer lives.

AND A THIRD THING, which is really resource ownership rather than prompting: "use the connection
that exists". That is a lease/handle held somewhere both askers can see, not a prompt at all.
Naming it here so it is not solved by accident inside the prompt layer, where it does not belong.

NOT URGENT and deliberately unbuilt: the concrete customers (Serpro VPN, Teams, Outlook, Telegram,
WhatsApp) are the bridges the operator said should mature first. Filed so the primitive is designed
once, from three real cases, rather than three times from one.
